CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Amabile called the City Council Meeting to order at the hour of 6:01 p.m. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Police Chief Reyna led the pledge of allegiance. ROLL CALL – MEMBERS OF THE CITY COUNCIL PRESENT: Council Members Refugio LLamas – District 2, Marcus Chavez – District 3, Deborah Lewis – District 4, Mayor Michael Amabile, District 1 – vacant; ABSENT: None STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT: City Manager Than, City Attorney Lerner, City Clerk Mallonee, City Treasurer Lawrence, Community & Economic Development Director Souza Elms, Police Chief Reyna, Public Works Director Via, Fire Chief Dorenbush, Finance Director Moreno (participating via Zoom), Parks & Recreation Director Heim, Human Resources Director Carlos PRESENTATIONS. PROCLAMATION – RECOGNIZING JOE SOUSA FOR HIS PUBLIC SERVICE AND DEDICATION TO THE COMMUNITY OF LOS BANOS. Mayor Amabile presented the proclamation to Joe Sousa who was present to accept. PUBLIC FORUM: THIS TIME IS RESERVED FOR MEMBERS OF THE PUBLIC WHO WISH TO ADDRESS THE CITY COUNCIL ON ITEMS THAT ARE NOT ON THE AGENDA AND THAT ARE WITHIN THE SUBJECT MATTER JURISDICTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL. SPEAKERS MUST DIRECT THEIR COMMENTS TO THE CITY COUNCIL AND LIMIT THEIR COMMENTS TO NO MORE THAN THREE (3) MINUTES. IT IS REQUESTED THAT NO COMMENTS BE MADE DURING THIS PERIOD ON ITEMS ON THE AGENDA. THE PUBLIC WILL HAVE AN OPPORTUNITY TO COMMENT ON ITEMS ON THE AGENDA ONCE THE ITEM HAS BEEN CALLED AND THE MAYOR OPENS THE ITEM TO THE PUBLIC. THE CITY COUNCIL IS PROHIBITED BY LAW FROM TAKING ANY ACTION ON MATTERS DISCUSSED THAT ARE NOT ON THE AGENDA. NO ADVERSE CONCLUSIONS SHOULD BE DRAWN IF THE CITY COUNCIL DOES NOT RESPOND TO PUBLIC COMMENT AT THIS TIME. SPEAKERS ARE NOT ALLOWED TO SURRENDER/CEDE THEIR PUBLIC COMMENT TIME. Mayor Amabile opened the public forum. JOHN SPEVAK stated that it was a pleasure to be present for the presentation of a proclamation honoring Joe Sousa. He recognized Mr. Sousa’s longtime contributions to the City, including his work on the canal trail and his service on the Parks & Recreation and Tree Commissions for approximately 25 years. Mr. Spevak described Mr. Sousa as one of the 17 ITEM 7B City’s most dedicated and hardworking employees and expressed appreciation for his service to the community. BLANCHE JORGE, a downtown resident, spoke about September 11 and the role of search-and-rescue, police, bomb-detection, therapy, and recovery dogs during the events of that day. She also recognized the City’s animal shelter and noted that a rescue dog was identified and trained through the local shelter. MARIANA NIEVES, owner of Hippie Soul and founder of the Sunday Artisan Market, spoke about her experience operating a downtown business and creating opportunities for other small businesses through the market. She noted that many vendors have turned their market participation into businesses and stated that she encourages vendors to obtain the required permits and business licenses. She said the market brings hundreds of families downtown each Sunday and contributes to downtown revitalization and support of other local businesses. CARLOS FLORES, District 1, spoke regarding Mitzi Perez’s resignation and raised questions concerning the circumstances surrounding the resignation and an election-related investigation. He expressed concerns regarding County election processes, employment opportunities in Merced County, and the City’s hiring of an additional attorney, including the cost to taxpayers. NAOMI GUZMAN, District 1, thanked Mariana Nieves for establishing the Artisan Market and expressed concern about the limited activities available for local youth. She asked about the status of the proposed aquatic facility and expressed concerns regarding violence and bullying, youth activities, community events, employment opportunities, ongoing development, and the lack of progress on projects that have been discussed for several years. She also expressed concern regarding the condition of City streets and potholes. City Clerk Mallonee read letters from JULIE CREIGHTON and ANGELINA MENDOZA into the record. Ms. Creighton’s letter addressed the District 1 vacancy and expressed concerns regarding the selection of the next representative. Ms. Mendoza’s letter requested additional information regarding the City’s plans to address homelessness, including the One Tree project, emergency shelter capacity, services, and options for individuals currently experiencing unsheltered homelessness. No one else came forward to speak and the public forum was closed. CONSIDERATION OF APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA. Council Member LLamas requested a brief discussion regarding Item H – City Council Resolution No. 7156 – Approving the Purchase of One (1) BMW Police Motorcycle in the Amount of $44,301.91 from Long Beach BMW Motorcycles Through the State of California Contract No. 1-22-23-30 Motorcycles. The motion carried by the following vote: AYES: Chavez, Lewis, LLamas, Mayor Amabile; NOES: None; ABSENT: None. DISCUSSION AND DIRECTION OF CHROMIUM VI TREATMENT ENGINEERING REPORT. Public Works Director Via presented the staff report and introduced Kevin Berryhill, P.E., of Provost & Pritchard, who provided a PowerPoint presentation on the engineering report addressing chromium-6 in the City’s drinking water. Mr. Berryhill reviewed the chromium-6 regulations, the City’s compliance timeline, treatment alternatives that have been considered, recent pilot testing, and estimated costs. He explained that all 13 City wells exceed the State’s 10 parts per billion standard and that the City has received an extension to 2030 to address the issue. Mr. Berryhill discussed several treatment alternatives, including replacement wells, blending, surface water, ion exchange, reverse osmosis, and zerovalent iron. He explained that reduction-coagulation-filtration (RCF) was identified as the most viable option. The process converts soluble chromium-6 into a form that can be removed through filtration. Recent pilot testing successfully reduced chromium-6 levels below the State limit, although additional work is needed to address filter backwashing, waste handling, and water flushing during system startup. Based on the pilot testing, the estimated cost to treat an individual well ranges from approximately $2.7 million to $4.8 million, with an estimated total cost of approximately $42 million for all 13 wells. Annual operating costs are estimated at approximately $1.25 million. Mr. Berryhill recommended beginning with a full-scale treatment facility at Well 9, which would allow the City to address remaining issues, establish more accurate costs, and apply lessons learned to future facilities. City Manager Than discussed the City’s responsibility to provide clean drinking water, the complexity and cost of the new requirements, the need for additional funding and testing, and the fact that many other cities are facing similar chromium-6 issues. Council discussed the operation of the treatment system, the cost of the Well 9 facility, similar treatment systems in other cities, potential impacts of backwash water on the wastewater system, and the possibility of receiving additional extensions from the State Water Board. Mayor Amabile asked whether the pumps would go offline during filter backwashing. Mr. Berryhill explained that, depending on the number and configuration of filters, the system could continue producing water at a reduced rate while individual filters are being backwashed. Council Member Lewis asked about the estimated cost to treat all 13 wells and the cost of using Well 9 as the initial test site. City Manager Than stated that the estimated cost for Well 9 was approximately $4.5 million. Council Member Llamas asked whether similar treatment plants were currently in operation or planned. City Manager Than explained that other cities have different configurations, including hybrid systems, and that the treatment system will need to be configured and tested to meet the City’s specific needs. He also responded to questions regarding the impact of backwash water on the wastewater system and emphasized the importance of testing to determine the actual effects and treatment requirements. Council Member Chavez asked whether another extension of the compliance timeline could be possible given the significant cost and the need to further establish the treatment process. City Manager Than stated that the State Water Board has indicated that extensions may be possible, provided the City continues meeting the requirements of its approved compliance plan, and noted that the City is working closely with the Water Board. Mayor Amabile stated that the City wants to identify the best and most affordable solution for the City and its residents. City Manager Than stated that the full-scale pilot treatment facility at Well 9 was anticipated to begin in Spring 2027. 20 Mayor Amabile invited the public to come forward and speak; ANN McCAULEY spoke about her residential water conditioning system and reverse osmosis system and asked how such systems help address chromium-6 at the residential level. Mayor Amabile explained the function of reverse osmosis, and City Manager Than provided additional information regarding California’s drinking water standard compared with the standard used elsewhere in the nation. No other members of the public came forward to speak. No one else came forward to speak Consensus of the City Council to move forward with the recommendation to proceed with final design of the City’s first full scale pilot reduction-coagulation-filtration (RCF) treatment facility at Well 9, and pursue funding opportunities for implementation of the City’s chromium compliance program. CONSIDERATION OF ADOPTION OF CITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION NO. 7157 – CALLING AND GIVING NOTICE OF THE HOLDING OF A SPECIAL ELECTION ON TUESDAY, MARCH 2, 2027, TO FILL A VACANCY CREATED BY THE RESIGNATION OF COUNCILMEMBER MITZY PEREZ, AS REQUIRED BY THE PROVISIONS OF THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA RELATING TO GENERAL LAW CITIES. City Attorney Lerner presented the staff report and explained that Resolution No. 7157 would call a special election for March 2, 2027, to fill the District 1 City Council vacancy created by the resignation of Council Member Mitzy Perez and would consolidate the election with the Merced County election. She explained that State law requires the City Council to act within 60 days of the vacancy by either appointing a replacement or calling a special election. Because two current Council Members were appointed rather than elected, the Council cannot make another appointment without creating a majority of appointed Council Members; therefore, the vacancy must be filled by special election. She further explained that the March 2, 2027 election date meets the required 114-day timeframe for calling the election. The candidate filing period is expected to be November 7 through December 2, 2026, and the individual elected would serve the remainder of the term through the November 7, 2028 general election. The estimated cost of the special election is approximately $65,590, plus or minus 10%. Mayor Amabile invited the public to comment; no one came forward. Council Member LLamas stated that the vacancy was unfortunate and was no one’s fault. Mayor Amabile emphasized the importance of encouraging residents to vote, noting that voter turnout in the previous election for the seat was low. Motion by Chavez, seconded by LLamas to adopt City Council Resolution No. 7157 – Calling and Giving Notice of the Holding of a Special Election on Tuesday, March 2, 2027, to Fill a Vacancy Created by the Resignation of Councilmember Mitzy Perez, as Required by the Provisions of the Laws of the State of California Relating to General Law Cities. CONSIDERATION OF ADOPTION OF CITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION NO. 7158 – APPROVING PURCHASE AGREEMENTS WITH BURTONS FIRE APPARATUS FOR 21 THE PURCHASE OF TWO (2) ROSENBAUER TYPE I FIRE ENGINES IN THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF $1,839,615.39; AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE THE AGREEMENT; AND APPROVING BUDGET AMENDMENTS IN THE AMOUNT OF $1,246,615.39 IN MEASURE P FIRE FUND. Fire Chief Dorenbush presented the staff report, which included a PowerPoint presentation explaining that the Fire Department’s apparatus fleet has been aging, resulting in increased repair costs, reduced reliability, and greater downtime. The Department responds to approximately 4,000 calls annually from two stations, placing additional demands on the existing fleet. Chief Dorenbush stated that the City had an opportunity to purchase two immediately available Rosenbauer engines at a significantly reduced cost. The engines, which seat six firefighters and have 750-gallon tanks, could be delivered before November, avoiding the typical 18- to 24-month build time for new apparatus. He noted that the engines typically cost approximately $1.2 to $1.3 million each but were available for just under $1 million each. The total project cost is approximately $1.84 million, funded through the existing budget allocation, trade-ins of two command vehicles and two engines, and approximately $1.2 million in Measure P funds. Chief Dorenbush stated that the purchase would improve reliability and firefighter safety, reduce maintenance costs, and support the City’s fleet replacement program. One of the new engines would be assigned to the new Fire Station #4, with the current frontline apparatus moved to reserve status. Mayor Amabile invited the public to come forward to speak; no one came forward. Council Member Lewis congratulated the Fire Chief and the City on the opportunity to purchase the fire engines at a significant discount, noting the importance of reliable equipment to community safety. Council Member Chavez confirmed that one of the new engines would be assigned to Fire Station #4 and asked why the front bumper was so large and extended. Fire Chief Dorenbush explained that each jurisdiction has different specifications for its apparatus. Council Member Llamas stated that the purchase positions the City to provide greater public safety response and positions the City for the future. City Manager Than thanked the Measure P Oversight Committee for promptly reviewing the request and recommending approval of the Measure P funding. Mayor Amabile asked how much time would be saved by purchasing the available engines. Chief Dorenbush stated that the City would save approximately 18 to 24 months compared to ordering new apparatus, in addition to receiving the engines at a better price. Motion by Lewis seconded by LLamas to adopt City Council Resolution No. 7158 – Approving Purchase Agreements with Burtons Fire Apparatus for the Purchase of Two (2) Rosenbauer Type I Fire Engines in the Total Amount of $1,839,615.39; Authorizing the City Manager to Execute the Agreement; and Approving Budget Amendments in the Amount of $1,246,615.39 in Measure P Fire Fund. The project developer shall notify a qualified professional archaeologist. If the find is determined to be significant, appropriate mitigation measures shall be formulated and implemented. 36.
In the event of an accidental discovery or recognition of any human remains in any location other than a dedicated cemetery, the City shall ensure that this language is included in all permits in accordance with CEQA Guidelines section 15064.5( e ): If human remains are found during construction there shall be no further excavation or disturbance of the site or any nearby area reasonably suspected to overlie adjacent human remains until the Los Banos Police Department contacts the coroner of Merced County to determine that no investigation of the cause of death is required. If the coroner determines the remains to be Native American, the coroner shall contact the Native American Heritage Commission within 24 hours. The Native American Heritage Commission shall identify the person or persons it believes to be the most likely descendent from the deceased Native American. The most likely descendent may then make recommendations to the landowner or the person responsible for the excavation work, for means of treating or disposing of, with appropriate dignity, the human remains and associated grave goods as provided in Public Resources Code Section 5097.98. The landowner or his authorized representative shall rebury the Native American human remains and associated grave goods with appropriate dignity on the property in a location not subject to further disturbance if: a) the Native American Heritage Commission is unable to identify a most likely descendent or the most likely descendent failed to make a recommendation within 24 hours after being notified by the commission; b) the descendent identified fails to make a recommendation; or c) the landowner or his authorized representative rejects the recommendation of the descendent, and the mediation by the Native American Heritage Commission fails to provide measures acceptable to the landowner. 66.

67.
Prior to approval of Improvement Plans or Final Maps, the developer shall obtain any necessary easements for utilities across adjoining properties.
68.
All existing overhead utilities shall be placed underground with the exception of high voltage power lines. No new overhead utility lines and equipment shall be shown on Improvement Plans and Grading Plans.
69.

70.

Developer shall install street lights to meet the illumination standards required in the City street light standards.
71.
If capacity of public sewer/water facilities required to service this tract are deemed insufficient, the developer may be required to upgrade facilities as necessary.
72.
The proposed project shall conform to the requirements of the Los Banos Water Master Plan, including payment of the water connection impact fee.
73.
Approved backflow devices shall be installed as required.
74.
Domestic water services shall not be placed in driveways.
75.

The developer shall construct all on-site and off-site sewer facilities necessary to serve the project, subject to reimbursement for over-sizing, as determined by the City.
77.
Prior to submission of improvement plans for the first phase of development, a Master Sewer Plan for the development shall be submitted, reviewed, and approved by the City Engineer.

Upon issuance of a building permit, reimbursements for the San Luis Storm Line and Basin at Talbot Park Reimbursement shall be payable to the City of Los Banos in the amount of $858.61 per unit.

102.

103.

Awarding the De Anza Way/State Route 165 Access Improvements project contract to Cal Valley Construction, Inc.; and 2. Authorizing the City Manager to execute the Construction Contract Agreement in the amount of $670,402.00; and 3. Authorizing the Public Works Director to administer the Construction Contract, including a 15% contingency of $100,560.30; and 4. Amending the 26/27 Fiscal Year budget increasing the Measure V Fund (214-430-210-716) by $398,058.53 to cover the increased cost of the lowest responsible bid, the contingency, and construction support.
Background: The De Anza Way/State Route 165 Access Improvements Project was developed to address existing traffic circulation, access, and safety needs at the intersection of De Anza Way and State Route 165. The improvements are intended to enhance vehicle movements, provide safer pedestrian access, and improve access to adjacent properties. The project generally includes roadway improvements, intersection modifications, grading, paving, drainage improvements, traffic control devices, signage, striping, and 69 ITEM 7D other associated work necessary to improve access between De Anza Way and State Route 165. Discussion: The major work consists of reconstructing the 3-way intersection of De Anza Way and State Route 165 within the City of Los Banos. The project improvements include adding a right turn lane, curb, gutter, and sidewalk to northbound State Route 165; grinding and overlaying the existing State Route 165 pavement; pavement delineation and signage additions; constructing curb ramps at the intersection corners; and constructing a splitter island along De Anza Way at the intersection. Staff enlisted the services of Mark Thomas Company to design the project. The project was released for advertisement on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. The bid opening was held on Wednesday, August 26, 2026. The Public Works Department, through the office of the City Clerk, received seven (7) bids from the following contractors: Cal Valley Construction, Inc. Fresno, CA $670,402.00 Terra West Construction Clovis, CA $694,122.56 Granite Construction Co Fresno, CA $720,702.00 Tom Mayo Construction, Inc. Stockton, CA $790,980.00 Avison Construction, Inc. Madera, CA $803,770.00 Machado & Sons Construction, Inc. Turlock, CA $807,039.00 United Pavement Maintenance Hughson, CA $855,702.80 Staff reviewed each of the bid proposals for completeness. Cal Valley Construction, Inc. has provided the lowest responsive and responsible bid for the project. Staff is recommending Cal Valley Construction, Inc., be awarded the contract for the construction of the De Anza Way/State Route 165 Access Improvements. Staff is recommending a contingency of fifteen percent (15%) to address any unforeseen conditions or issues that may arise during construction. The administration of this contract, including the 15% contingency, is to be performed by the Public Works Director. Environmental Analysis: The Shaunessy Village subdivision and associated circulation improvements, including the De Anza Way connection to Mercey Springs Road (SR 165), were previously evaluated in the Spadafore-Giannone Area Plan Mitigated Negative Declaration (SCH #2005071027), adopted by the City Council on December 7, 2005, and a subsequent CEQA Addendum for the modified subdivision map and street layout. The proposed project consists solely of opening the existing De Anza Way connection as a right-in/right-out access point and does not increase development intensity, alter land uses, or authorize new construction beyond what was previously approved and analyzed. A traffic operations study concluded that the opening access would redistribute traffic within the existing roadway network, allow for better emergency response time, and would 70 maintain or improve operations at nearby intersections without creating significant transportation impacts. Staff has determined that the previously adopted environmental documents adequately address the proposed action and that no substantial changes, changed circumstances, or new information exist that would require additional environmental review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15162 and 15164. Therefore, no further environmental review is required. Fiscal Impact: Funds for this project have been programmed in Traffic Impact Fund account 230-430-220-716, and Measure V account 214-430-210-716 in the 2026-2027 Fiscal Year budget. The proposed amendment will increase the amount in the Measure V Fund (214-430-210-716) by $398,058.53 to cover the increased cost of the lowest responsible bid, the contingency, and construction support. Background: During the fiscal year 2026-2027 budget preparation the Public Works Department identified equipment and vehicles needed for staff to effectively and efficiently perform the duties assigned to the department. Acquisitions and replacement items have been identified as necessary for safety, efficiency, productivity, and/or environmental reasons (Air Board CARB Compliance). Listed below are the equipment that staff is requesting to purchase: • 27ST0003 – Steel Roller Compactor: This steel roller compactor acquisition will support various internal street pavement projects. Purchasing this equipment will eliminate the need to rent a roller from outside vendors, increasing equipment availability, and improving operational efficiency. This is funded in the Streets budget account 100-431-210-753.
• 27WA0007 – Hydro Excavator Truck: This hydro excavator acquisition will support Public Works maintenance activities by providing increased safety, precision, and operational efficiency. The equipment will improve the ability to perform excavation and utility-related work while minimizing risks and enhancing overall productivity. This is equally funded 83 ITEM 7E in Water and Wastewater Collections budget accounts 501-461-100-755 & 502-432-100-755. • 27WA0008 – Backhoe: This backhoe assists Staff with digging, handling and loading in their daily tasks and projects. This is equally funded in the Water and Wastewater Collections budget accounts 501-461-100-753 & 502-432-100-753. • 27WC0003 – Sewer Truck: Replaces a 2014 Sewer Truck that is experiencing increasing repair costs, reliability issues, and performance limitations, helping to ensure dependable service and reduce ongoing maintenance expenses. This is equally funded in the Water and Wastewater Collections budget accounts 501-461-100-755 & 502-432-100-755. Discussion: The City of Los Banos is a member of Sourcewell cooperative procurement agency (membership #60888). Sourcewell (formerly NJPA) is a public agency serving as a national municipal contracting agency established under the Service Cooperative statute by Minnesota Legislative Statute with the authority to develop and offer cooperative procurement services to its membership, which includes states, cities, counties, and other government and public agencies. Per the statute [Minn. Stat. § 123A.21 Subd. 4 (2017)], Sourcewell facilitates a competitive bidding and contracting process on behalf of the needs of itself and its members, resulting in Cooperative Purchasing. Sourcewell contracts are awarded by the action of the Sourcewell Board of Directors based on the open and competitive bidding process. As a member of Sourcewell, the City of Los Banos can select vendors, selected by Sourcewell, without further competitive bidding. City Code Sec. 3-10.290 allows for the use of cooperative procurement: (b) Use of another entity’s contract. The City Manager may authorize the procurement of commodities, equipment and/or services through the use of a contract initiated by another governmental, public agency, provided that the original parties to the contract agree, the contract was awarded within twelve (12) months of the date of authorization, the contract is for identical or nearly identical goods and/or services, and the contract resulted from a competitive bid using methods similar to those required by this chapter. (§1, Ord. 1068, eff. February 1, 2008. The City of Los Banos has previously utilized cooperative procurement through Sourcewell to make purchases. This procurement method has demonstrated efficiency and effectiveness in acquiring equipment for the Public Works Department. Cooperative procurement enables the City to obtain competitive pricing while streamlining the purchasing process by eliminating repetitive, resource-intensive, and costly competitive bidding procedures. Currently, project information is managed across multiple systems, spreadsheets, emails, and paper-based processes, creating inefficiencies, delays, and inconsistent record-keeping. After reviewing several construction management platforms, staff identified Procore as a comprehensive solution that best meets the City’s needs. Procore is a cloud-based platform that centralizes project information, streamlines workflows, improves collaboration between office and field teams, enhances budget and schedule oversight, and provides better documentation and transparency for reporting and audits. Implementation will advance the City’s goals of increasing efficiency, reducing project risks, and improving delivery of public infrastructure projects. The benefits of this software include: 117 ITEM 7G 1. Centralized Project Oversight o Manages all capital improvement and public works projects in one system. o Tracks progress across multiple projects (roads, utilities, buildings, etc.). o Improves visibility for both internal departments and external stakeholders. 2. Enhanced Collaboration with Contractors & Consultants o Connects City staff, consultants, contractors, and inspectors in real time. o Ensures everyone has the latest documents and updates, reducing miscommunication. o Reduces reliance on emails, calls, or in-person meetings. 3. Improved Contract & Document Management o Centralizes RFIs (Request for Information), submittals, change orders, and meeting minutes. o Maintains a complete audit trail for accountability and FOIA compliance. 4. Financial Oversight & Budget Tracking o Tracks project costs in real time against budgets. o Forecasts and manages change orders to prevent overruns. o Integrates with municipal accounting systems. 5. Field Inspections & Daily Logs o Allows inspectors to log notes, photos, and observations directly from the field. o Speeds up responses to jobsite issues and ensures accurate records. 6. Transparency & Reporting o Provides customizable dashboards and reporting tools. o Keeps City leadership, Council, and the public informed on timelines and budgets. o Strengthens public reporting and audit readiness. 7. Regulatory & Compliance Management o Maintains organized records for audits, inquiries, and legal protections. o Ensures documentation is properly archived for long-term asset management. 8. Standardized Processes Across Projects o Promotes consistent workflows across engineering, public works, and procurement. o Reduces onboarding time with repeatable templates and forms. 9. Integration with Other City Systems o Compatible with ESRI GIS, asset management systems, and ERP/accounting tools. o Reduces manual entry and duplication of data. 10. Public Trust & Accountability o Demonstrates responsible stewardship of taxpayer funds. o Supports smoother audits, grant compliance, and capital improvement planning. 118 Discussion: Staff recommends continuing the City’s use of Procore Project Management Software to strengthen the planning, delivery, and oversight of capital improvement and infrastructure projects. Procore centralizes project documentation, provides real-time tracking, and improves communication among City staff, consultants, contractors, and field personnel. The platform’s budgeting, scheduling, reporting, mobile access, and automated workflow tools will help reduce errors, minimize delays, improve accountability, and allow field staff to upload inspections, photos, and updates directly from the jobsite. Automated routing for RFIs and change orders, standardized templates, customizable dashboards, and integration with City systems will further improve efficiency, consistency, and transparency while reducing duplication of effort. Staff reviewed other project management platforms, including Microsoft Project and Trello; however, Procore is designed specifically for construction and public works project delivery. Its tools include inspection logs, prevailing wage tracking, DocuSign integration, and unlimited user access. Procore is used by several public agencies, including the counties of Santa Clara, San Mateo, and San Joaquin, as well as Cal Fire, the City of Roseville, and the City of Lathrop. The agreement provides enough user access for Public Works staff to fully utilize the system and extends access to Planning staff, improving interdepartmental coordination on critical projects. The agreement also includes onboarding and training provided by Procore staff. Procurement was completed through EC America, Inc. under the California Multiple Award Schedules (CMAS) program, a procurement program managed by the California Department of General Services. This process provides a compliant and streamlined purchasing method consistent with state procurement requirements. The agreement has also been reviewed by the City Attorney. On September 3, 2025, City Council approved a one-year contract for Procore to allow staff to implement the software and evaluate its effectiveness. Since then, staff has found Procore to be a valuable tool for project coordination, document control, communication, and accountability. Approval of a three-year renewal will allow the City to continue using the platform without interruption, maintain consistent project management practices, and support long-term planning for current and future capital improvement projects. For these reasons, staff recommends approval of the three-year renewal agreement. 119 Fiscal Impact: The annual cost of use per year is $24,104.74, with an approximate cost of $72,314.22 for the next three years. Once Procore receives an error ticket as reported from Customer, Procore shall provide Customer with timely status updates as reasonably determined by Procore until a workaround or other resolution is established by Procore. 134 Agenda Staff Report TO: Mayor Amabile and City Council Members FROM: Soknirorn Than, City Manager DATE: September 16, 2026 TYPE OF REPORT: Consent Item SUBJECT: Approval of an Amendment with Mid Valley IT to Upgrade City Hall Server Recommendation: It is recommended that the City Council adopts the Resolution approving an amendment to the agreement with Mid Valley IT to upgrade City Hall Server in the amount of $335,344.35 and authorizing the City Manager to execute the amendment including the contingency of 10% in the amount of $33,534.00. Background: The City of Los Banos currently contracts for managed IT services to support daily operations, cybersecurity, infrastructure maintenance, and technology planning. The City issued a request for updated service proposals to ensure continuity of service and compliance with new operational and legislative requirements, including SB 707. Mid Valley IT has provided a comprehensive proposal for a fixed monthly managed services agreement, along with additional audio/visual upgrades required for SB 707 compliance. On March 18, 2026, the City Council approved a Managed IT Services Agreement with Mid Valley IT effective April 1, 2026, for a three-year term. Under the agreement, Mid Valley IT provides comprehensive managed information technology services, including unlimited remote and on-site technical support, regular onsite visits, network documentation, capital planning assistance, antivirus hosting and monitoring, a standard 48-hour response time for service requests, and a four-hour response time for emergency issues.
135 ITEM 7H The agreement establishes a fixed monthly service fee of $12,877, subject to a 3.5% annual cost-of-living adjustment. In addition to the base support services, the City may utilize optional subscription-based technology services, including endpoint detection and response (EDR) antivirus protection, Duo multi-factor authentication, Inky email filtering, Microsoft 365 licensing at published Microsoft rates, and managed backup services currently billed at $2,380 per month. The agreement was intended to provide predictable IT support costs and ensure ongoing maintenance, cybersecurity monitoring, technology planning, and operational support for the City's information technology infrastructure. Discussion: The City Hall server infrastructure is a critical component of the City's information technology environment, supporting daily operations, data storage, business applications, cybersecurity functions, and interdepartmental communications. Much of the City's existing server and storage environment has reached the point where replacement and modernization are necessary to maintain system reliability, improve performance, and support future technology needs. The proposed project would replace the current server cluster and storage platform with a modern, centralized infrastructure consisting of new Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) servers, a Storage Area Network (SAN), high-speed network switching equipment, and an upgraded backup environment. The project also includes migration of existing virtual servers, implementation of a clustered server architecture, and upgrades of approximately 18 virtual machines to Windows Server 2025. A key benefit of the proposed upgrade is the establishment of a centralized management platform for both network and storage resources. Centralized administration will allow Information Technology staff and the City's managed service provider to more efficiently monitor system health, manage security updates, allocate storage resources, and respond to operational issues. The upgraded environment will improve scalability, simplify maintenance activities, and reduce the risk associated with aging hardware and fragmented storage systems. This centralized approach allows for a unified system to branch facilities such as the new Development Services Center (at the old PD Annex Building), and the Fire Station No. 4. This will lower cost for firewall and subscriptions. The project also enhances the City's cybersecurity and disaster recovery capabilities. The addition of a dedicated backup appliance, modern storage architecture, and updated server operating systems will strengthen data protection, improve system resiliency, and support business continuity in the event of equipment failure, cybersecurity incidents, or other service disruptions. The proposed solution includes two enterprise-grade HPE data center switches, an HPE MSA 2070 SAN with high-performance solid-state storage, four new HPE ProLiant Gen12 servers configured in a clustered environment, Windows Server 2025 licensing, and 136 associated implementation services. Mid Valley IT will provide professional services to design, install, configure, and migrate the City's virtual server environment to the new platform. The total project cost is $335,344.35 including equipment, software licensing, labor, sales tax, and installation services. Staff is requesting a 10% contingency in the amount of $33,534.00 to allow for unforeseen conditions associated with this upgrade. Staff believes the proposed investment is necessary to ensure the continued reliability, security, and performance of the City's core technology infrastructure while providing a scalable platform capable of supporting future service delivery, operational efficiency, and technology modernization initiatives. Procurement: Pursuant to Los Banos Municipal Code Section 3-10.230, staff recommends utilizing noncompetitive negotiation for the procurement of the City Hall Server Cluster and Network Infrastructure Upgrade. The proposed purchase qualifies under multiple provisions of Section 3-10.230, including: 1. Technology products, including enterprise servers, storage area network (SAN) equipment, network switching infrastructure, virtualization software, and associated licensing. 2. Additions to and maintenance of existing equipment that can be more efficiently performed by a particular company with knowledge of the City's existing environment. 3. Equipment that must be compatible with existing systems, network architecture, virtualization platforms, cybersecurity controls, and operational procedures supported by the City's managed information technology services provider. Mid Valley IT currently serves as the City's managed IT services provider under a long-term support agreement and is responsible for maintaining the City's network, server infrastructure, cybersecurity systems, backups, and daily technology operations. The proposed solution was specifically designed to integrate with the City's existing environment and includes migration of approximately 18 virtual servers, implementation of centralized storage, and configuration of a new clustered server architecture. Utilizing Mid Valley IT for this project provides continuity of operations, minimizes implementation risk, reduces system downtime during migration, and ensures compatibility with the City's existing technology infrastructure. Consistent with Section 3-10.230, staff finds that the proposed procurement involves specialized technology products and system upgrades that must be integrated with existing infrastructure and supported by the City's current managed service provider. Staff further finds that the proposed procurement is in the City's best interest because it provides a complete, integrated solution that enhances reliability, cybersecurity, centralized management, and long-term operational efficiency while reducing the risks associated with transitioning critical infrastructure to an unfamiliar vendor. 137 Fiscal Impact: Funding for this upgrade is budgeted for within the Information Technology Division for Fiscal Year 2026-2027 in account 610-410-100-770 for a total amount of $400,000.00. Customer Initials 152 Agenda Staff Report TO: Mayor Amabile and City Council Members FROM: Stacy Souza Elms, Community and Economic Development Director DATE: September 16, 2026 TYPE OF REPORT: Agenda Item SUBJECT: Approval of a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF, Inc. for Building and Fire Prevention Services and Authorization for the City Manager to Execute the Agreement ______________________________________________________________________ Recommendation: Adopt a Resolution approving a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF, Inc. for Building and Fire Prevention Services and authorizing the City Manager to execute the Agreement. Background: The City released a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for Building and Fire Prevention Services on April 8, 2026, seeking a qualified consultant to provide comprehensive building and fire prevention services, including an on-call Certified Building Official, permit processing, plan review, inspections, code enforcement support, and related administrative functions. Proposals were due on May 6, 2026. The RFQ indicated that qualifications would be evaluated based on consultant experience, organizational approach, staff availability, past performance, and overall qualifications. The City received five (5) Statements of Qualifications from the following firms: 1. True North Compliance Services 2. CSG Consultants, Inc.
3. Bureau Veritas North America 4. 4LEAF, Inc.
153 ITEM 8 5. Shums Coda Associates The RFQ evaluation process was conducted in accordance with the evaluation criteria established in the solicitation documents. The City reviewed the qualifications, staffing resources, municipal experience, service delivery capabilities, and overall ability of each firm to meet the City's operational needs. The RFQ specifically emphasized staff availability, qualifications and experience, project approach, and demonstrated success providing services to public agencies. Based on the evaluation of qualifications and experience, staff determined that 4LEAF, Inc. was the most qualified firm to provide the requested services. 4LEAF demonstrated extensive experience providing contract building department services throughout California and possesses the staffing resources and technical capabilities necessary to support the City's development review and permitting activities. Staff subsequently negotiated a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF that reflects the service requirements identified in the RFQ and is in the best interest of the City. Discussion: Under the proposed agreement, 4LEAF will provide comprehensive building and fire prevention services including: • Certified Building Official services; • Building permit processing and administration; • Building and fire plan review services; • Building inspection services; • Building code enforcement support; • Accessibility review services; • On-call and emergency response services; and • Support for the City's electronic permitting and Tyler Technologies systems. The agreement includes performance standards and review timelines intended to ensure efficient permit processing and customer service. The consultant will provide qualified personnel with the necessary certifications and experience to maintain continuity of operations and respond to fluctuating development activity levels. The proposed agreement has an initial term of one year beginning in September 2026 and ending in September 2027, with two optional one-year extensions exercisable by the City. Fiscal Impact: The agreement is funded through building permit, plan review, and inspection fees collected by the City. Compensation is structured primarily as a percentage of fees collected for building permit processing and related services, with hourly rates applicable for special or requested services. The cost of services will be paid from available Building 154 Division revenues and is anticipated to be offset by fees collected for development services. Additionally, there is a $80,640.00 start up cost that is appropriated for the implementation of Energov Tyler Technology. This is to implement the new permitting system in preparation for the One-Stop Shop permitting system. Background: State legislative and regulatory actions have a significant impact on municipal operations, funding, service delivery, infrastructure development, housing, public safety, environmental compliance, and economic development. As Los Banos continues to grow, state policies increasingly influence the City's ability to address local priorities and deliver services efficiently to residents and businesses. The City has historically engaged with state legislators, regional partners, advocacy organizations, and state agencies to advance local priorities and secure funding opportunities. Adoption of an annual legislative platform provides a framework for those advocacy efforts and allows the City to respond in a timely manner to legislation and budget proposals during the legislative session. The proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 Legislative Priorities were developed by Nossaman LLP, our state advocacy partner, based on City Council goals, General Plan objectives, adopted budget priorities, infrastructure needs, public safety objectives, and operational 179 ITEM 9 responsibilities. The platform is intended to remain broad enough to address evolving legislative issues while providing clear policy direction. Discussion: The legislative platform establishes guiding principles that enable the City to respond efficiently and consistently to emerging legislative issues while advancing Council priorities and community interests. The platform focuses on six (6) key policy areas: 1. Fiscal Stability, Local Control, and Core Services a. The platform supports preserving local control over land use, public services, infrastructure planning, and fiscal decisions that are best addressed by locally elected officials. The City advocates for the protection of locally generated revenues, adequate funding for state-mandated programs, and regulatory flexibility that allows local governments to implement state requirements in a practical and cost-effective manner. These priorities help ensure that Los Banos can continue providing essential services, including public safety, street maintenance, water and wastewater operations, parks, and community development services while maintaining long-term fiscal sustainability. 2. Water, Sustainability, and Environmental Resources a. Reliable access to safe drinking water remains one of the City's most critical responsibilities. The platform supports state investments and policies that strengthen water quality compliance, groundwater sustainability, drought resilience, recycled water development, stormwater management, and regional water supply planning. The City also supports funding and technical assistance to address emerging contaminants and environmental requirements while minimizing financial impacts on ratepayers. Additionally, the platform recognizes the importance of climate resilience, emergency preparedness, and protecting community assets from natural and environmental hazards. 3. Economic Development, Downtown, and Local Jobs a. Economic growth is essential to maintaining a healthy local economy and expanding opportunities for residents. The legislative platform supports policies and programs that promote business attraction and retention, workforce development, infrastructure readiness, small business support, and job creation. The City also seeks investment in downtown revitalization, public improvements, tourism, arts, culture, and placemaking initiatives that strengthen Downtown Los Banos as a community gathering place and economic center. These efforts support a diversified tax base and help ensure that growing inland communities receive equitable consideration in statewide economic development programs. 4. Housing, Growth, and Neighborhood Quality 180 a. Los Banos continues to experience significant growth and housing demand. The platform supports policies that encourage the development of attainable and affordable housing while recognizing the corresponding need for infrastructure, transportation improvements, public safety services, parks, and other community facilities. The City advocates for preserving local planning authority and ensuring that housing production requirements remain balanced with community character, infrastructure capacity, and neighborhood compatibility. The platform also supports practical solutions and funding opportunities related to homelessness, behavioral health services, substance abuse treatment, domestic violence prevention, and youth services. 5. Streets, Transportation, Utilities, and Public Facilities a. The City has substantial ongoing needs related to roadway maintenance, traffic safety improvements, utility infrastructure, stormwater systems, parks, public facilities, and technology investments. The legislative platform supports increased and sustainable funding sources for capital improvements, maintenance programs, and infrastructure modernization efforts. The City also seeks grant opportunities and financing tools that help fund critical projects while minimizing impacts on local taxpayers and utility ratepayers. Transportation investments that improve safety, reduce congestion, and enhance regional connectivity are particularly important to supporting future growth and economic development. 6. Public Safety and Emergency Response a. Protecting residents and businesses remains a core City responsibility. The platform supports legislation and funding that strengthen police, fire, emergency medical, and disaster response capabilities. Priority areas include maintaining emergency response times, recruiting and retaining qualified personnel, investing in equipment and facilities, enhancing emergency preparedness, and supporting crime prevention initiatives. The City also recognizes the importance of youth programs, behavioral health services, violence prevention strategies, and community-based partnerships that address root causes of crime and improve neighborhood safety. Investments in emergency operations, disaster recovery, critical infrastructure protection, and mutual aid capabilities further support the City's commitment to public safety and community resilience. Fiscal Impact: Adoption of the Legislative Priorities does not have a direct fiscal impact. However, the platform provides guidance for pursuing grant funding, advocating for state budget appropriations, influencing legislation affecting municipal finances, and seeking resources that may reduce future costs or support City infrastructure and service needs. 181 Reviewed by: _______________________________ _______________________________ Mary Lerner, City Attorney Minerva Moreno, Finance Director Attachment: 1. Project Update: The City of Los Banos is advancing the renovation and adaptive reuse of the former Police Annex building located at 535 J Street into a new Development Services Center and City Hall Annex. The project will consolidate Community and Economic Development, Building, Public Works Administration, Engineering, Fire Prevention, and related public-facing services into a centralized location designed to improve customer service, accessibility, and operational efficiency. The existing two-story building contains approximately 11,255 square feet and is located within the Downtown Mixed-Use area. The project includes interior renovations to create public service counters, customer waiting areas, meeting spaces, staff workstations, and administrative offices. Exterior improvements include modernization of the building façade, landscaping, pedestrian walkways, parking lot enhancements, public art, and a public plaza that will create a more inviting civic presence in the downtown area. The project reuses an existing public facility without expanding the building footprint and maintains the site's established circulation patterns and municipal office use. 191 ITEM 10 On September 9, 2026, the Planning Commission considered and approved Site Plan Review No. 2026-08 and determined the project to be categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Existing Facilities). Next Steps: The project team is currently completing the Schematic Design phase of the project. The approved schematic design will be further refined through construction document preparation and cost estimating as part of the City's Progressive Design-Build process. The current project schedule anticipates completion of schematic design in October 2026, followed by preparation of construction documents and development of a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) proposal. Staff will be returning to the City Council with the final project design, project budget updates, and a GMP contract amendment for Council consideration and authorization to proceed with construction. Fiscal Impact: The Development Services Center project is funded through appropriations included in the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget. Background: On December 3, 2025, the County of Merced released a Request for Proposals (RFP) No. 7646, for funding available through the State of California’s HHAP Program to support Rapid Rehousing activities. The HHAP Program provides flexible funding to cities, counties, and Continuums of Care to assist individuals experiencing homelessness and increase access to housing and supportive services. On December 22, 2025, the City of Los Banos submitted a proposal in response to the County’s RFP. On February 4, 2026, the County issued an Intent to Negotiate letter notifying the City that its proposal had been ranked the highest and selected for funding in the amount of $134,500.00. 201 ITEM 11 The funding will support Rapid Rehousing activities, including rental deposits, rental application fees, landlord engagement, and landlord incentives. While the primary focus of the funding will be to support residents housed through the One Tree Permanent Supportive Housing project, the funds may also be used to assist eligible individuals residing in other rental housing throughout the community. On August 11, 2026, the County submitted the draft agreement to the City for review. The agreement has since been reviewed by the City Attorney and Finance Director and is now presented to the City Council for approval and authorization of execution by the City Manager. Discussion: The City's Housing Division is responsible for coordinating local efforts to address homelessness. Services include outreach and engagement, case management, housing navigation, and connections to supportive services, benefits, healthcare, and housing resources. The Housing Division also actively pursues grant funding opportunities to expand housing options and services for individuals experiencing homelessness. According to County Continuum of Care 2026 Point-in-Time Count, 101 individuals experiencing homelessness were identified within the City of Los Banos. Approval of the HHAP contract will provide additional resources to remove common barriers to housing, including rental deposits and application costs. The funding will also support landlord engagement efforts and incentive programs designed to increase housing opportunities for individuals experiencing homelessness. These resources will enhance the City's ability to successfully place eligible individuals into permanent housing, including units within the One Tree Permanent Supportive Housing development. The proposed contract will provide $134,500 in grant funding to support rapid rehousing efforts and assist individuals experiencing homelessness in obtaining and maintaining permanent housing. Fiscal Impact: There is no impact to the General Fund. Acceptance of the HHAP grant will increase both revenues and expenditures by $134,500 in Fiscal Year 2026-27. Grant revenue will be recognized in Account No. 100-000-339-010 (Other Grants), with corresponding expenditures appropriated in Account No. 100-419-130-273 (Special Departmental Expense) for eligible HHAP program activities. CTI is a time-limited, evidence-based case management model designed to support individuals who are experiencing homelessness or other major life transitions. CTI focuses on providing intensive support in the early stages of a transition to ensure that individuals do not experience setbacks or crises that could derail their progress. The key components of CTI include time-limited support, strengthening social supports, collaboration with other services, gradual reduction of support, and a focus on crisis prevention. I. Employ Motivational Interviewing (MI) techniques. MI is a client-centered, collaborative counseling approach designed to help individuals explore and resolve ambivalence about behavior change. The goal is to enhance a person's intrinsic motivation to make positive changes by creating an empathetic and non-judgmental environment. MI is often used in situations where individuals may be uncertain or resistant to change, such as in addressing substance use, mental health issues, or behaviors linked to chronic conditions. The key components of MI include expressing empathy, identifying discrepancies, rolling with resistance, supporting self-efficacy, elicit change talk, and autonomy and choice. J. Employ Harm Reduction techniques. Harm Reduction is an approach aimed at minimizing the negative consequences associated with certain behaviors, particularly those that are risky or potentially harmful, such as substance use. Rather than focusing solely on eliminating the behavior (such as requiring individuals to stop using drugs or alcohol), harm reduction acknowledges that some individuals may not be ready or able to stop immediately. The key 226 21 components of Harm Reduction include a non-judgmental approach, focus on practical strategies, health and safety over abstinence, empowerment and choice, holistic and person-centered approaches, and collaboration and support. Program Outcomes The California System Performance Measures (CA SPMs) are a standardized set of metrics to help assess progress towards preventing, reducing, and ending homelessness. The Contractor shall maintain or improve the following relevant CA SPMs for the contracted program. Measure 1a: The number of people accessing services who are experiencing homelessness. 246 41 Defining Factors: This measure is evaluated in comparison with the number of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness as identified in CA SPM 1b. Improvements: If the number of people served under CA SPM 1a increases by a rate greater than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that the program is reaching and supporting more people than before. If the number of people served under CA SPM 1a decreases by a rate that is the same or less than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less services needed and that access is declining proportionally. Measure 1b: The estimated number of people experiencing unsheltered homelessness on the CoC’s Point-in-Time Count (on a single day in the last week of January). Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less people experiencing unsheltered homelessness. Measure 2: The number of persons entering the system who are experiencing homelessness for the first time. Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people accessing services who are experiencing homelessness for the first time (defined as not accessing services while experiencing homelessness in the past two years). This measure is evaluated in comparison with the number of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness as identified in CA SPM 1b. Improvements: If the number of people served under CA SPM 2 increases by a rate greater than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that the program is reaching and supporting more people than before. If the number of people served under CA SPM 2 decreases by a rate that is the same or less than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less services needed and that access is declining proportionally. Measure 3: The number of people exiting homelessness into permanent housing. 247 42 Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people exiting homelessness into permanent housing, including people who exited the homelessness response system to permanent housing and people who moved into permanent housing within the homelessness response system. Improvement: An increase in CA SPM 3. This would indicate that there is an increase in permanent housing outcomes both inside and outside the homelessness response system. Measure 4: Length of time persons remained homeless. Defining Factors: This is measured by the average length of time (in number of days) that people were enrolled in street outreach (SO) or other non-residential projects (while experiencing homelessness), emergency shelter (ES), transitional housing (TH), and safe haven (SH) projects, as well as time during which people were enrolled in, but had not yet moved into, rapid rehousing (RRH), permanent supportive housing (PSH), and other permanent housing (OPH) projects. Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 4. This would indicate that there is a decrease in the length of time people experience homelessness while accessing services. Measure 5: Number of persons who return to homelessness after exiting homelessness to permanent housing. Defining Factors: This is measured by the percentage of people who return to homelessness within six months of exiting the homelessness response system to permanent housing. Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 5. This would indicate that people experiencing homelessness are being provided adequate services to maintain their permanent housing. Measure 6: Successful placements from street outreach. Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people with successful placements from street outreach projects, which includes exits to an emergency shelter (ES), safe haven (SH), transitional housing (TH), or permanent housing (PH) destinations. Improvement: An increase in CA SPM 6. This would indicate the success of street outreach in connecting people to shelter, interim, or permanent housing solutions. 248 43 The AE shall monitor progress for the CA SPMs utilizing the System Administrator Report [HUDX-223-AD] System Performance Measures within HMIS. The Contractor shall utilize and integrate the Merced City and County Continuum of Care (Merced CoC) Coordinated Entry System (CES) into program processes and operations. Program processes and operations shall comply with the Merced CoC CES Policy and Procedures. 257 52 The Contractor shall utilize the Merced CoC designated assessment tool. The Contractor shall make referrals to and receive referrals from the CES. This includes presenting individual cases, as applicable, at the CES meetings to determine appropriate service provider(s) referral(s). The Contractor shall collaborate with community partners, service providers, and local governmental agencies to case manage and provide unduplicated services. The Contractor shall attend and actively participate in the CES meetings as scheduled by the CES Lead. These meetings are conducted to discuss client needs and identify resources to help house and/or stabilize the individual. 20. CoC Meetings The Contractor shall attend and participate in the monthly Merced City and County Continuum of Care (CoC) meetings which occur on the first Thursday of each month. The Contractor shall maintain a good standing as a CoC General Member throughout the duration of this agreement. General Member requirements are detailed within the Merced CoC Governance Charter available on the Merced CoC website. 21. Annual Point-in-Time Count As required by HUD, CoC’s must conduct a “one-night, point-in-time” homeless count every other year during the last ten (10) days of January. The Merced CoC has opted to conduct this count annually. The Contractor may provide support for and be engaged in the Merced CoC annual Point-in-Time count. 22. Annual Housing Inventory Count As required by HUD, CoC’s must conduct a point-in-time inventory of programs that provide beds and units dedicated to serve people experiencing homelessness. The five program types included are Emergency Shelter, Transitional Housing, Rapid Re-Housing, Safe Haven, and Permanent Supportive Housing. The Contractor shall provide support for and be engaged in the data gathering, analysis, and submission of the Merced CoC Housing Inventory Count. 23. Project and Funding Sustainability When available and feasible, the Contractor shall make reasonable efforts to braid new and existing funding sources to sustain the project without duplicating any of the funding or services. Funding availability varies significantly from year to year. In the absence of available resources, the Contractor is highly encouraged to plan for obtaining the funding necessary for sustaining their project(s) during and beyond the term of this Agreement without supplanting funds. Leveraging available 258 53 funding sources is key to ensuring there isn’t a disruption of services to our clients and community members. 24. Inventory Management The Contractor shall establish controls to ensure adequate safeguards to prevent loss, damage, or theft to property, including equipment purchased with Agreement funds. If Contractor should no longer provide services under this Agreement, the equipment and property shall be returned to the AE. The Contractor shall be responsible for managing and tracking all supplies and equipment purchased with program funding. Fixed assets, IT equipment, and item purchases over $1,000.00 must be tagged and tracked. These items shall be inventoried by the Contractor at least annually and made available for review at the request of the AE. Items must be disposed of or surplus in compliance with terms and conditions of the funding sources used to purchase the item with prior notice and approval from the AE. All property including computer software, hardware, equipment, furniture, motorized items, and fixed assets purchased with AE funds must be returned to the AE following the termination of this Agreement. Thirty (30) days prior to the termination of this Agreement, all Contractor owned property shall be segregated from AE owned property. An inventory shall be conducted by Contractor and the AE to verify the proper separation and relinquishment of AE owned assets, equipment, supplies, and technical data/documentation. 25. Contractor’s Application for Funds The Contractor has applied through a Request for Proposal (RFP) submission for funding to provide the services outlined within this agreement. Contractor is entering into this Agreement on the basis of, and in substantial reliance upon, Contractor’s facts, information, assertions and representations contained within that application, and in any subsequent modifications or additions thereto. The Contractor warrants that all information, facts, assertions, and representations contained in the application and approved modifications and additions thereto are true, correct, and complete to the best of the Contractor’s knowledge. In the event that any part of the application and any approved modification and addition thereto is untrue, incorrect, incomplete, or misleading in such a manner that would substantially affect the approval, disbursement, or monitoring of the funding and the grants or activities governed by this agreement, then the AE may declare a breach hereof and take such action or pursue such remedies as are provided for breach hereof. 259 260
